passage: I'm Sharmila. At lunch today Minakshi wrinkled her nose when I opened my tiffin. It was methi paratha. My cheeks went hot and I shut the lid. I thought, she thinks my food is yucky. I stopped eating. Minakshi noticed and asked, “Did I do something?” I said, “You made a face at my lunch.” She looked around and laughed. “No! Someone at the next bench opened a boiled egg and it smells so strong!” I hadn't even noticed. She said, “Your paratha smells lovely, can I try a bit?”

qa.q: What was in Sharmila's tiffin?
qa.a: Her tiffin had methi paratha.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel when Minakshi wrinkled her nose, and what did she think it meant?
qa.a: She felt hurt and embarrassed, since her cheeks went hot and she shut the lid, thinking Minakshi found her food yucky. She had not noticed the smell from the next bench.

qa.q: How did Minakshi's question help?
qa.a: She asked, “Did I do something?” which let Sharmila say what she saw and let Minakshi explain the real reason.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt when she learned Sharmila thought it was about the paratha?
qa.a: Probably surprised and a bit sorry that her face had caused hurt. Her offer to try a bit shows she wanted to make it right.

grounding: A child sees a friend wrinkle her nose at lunch and feels hurt, but asking shows it was another smell.

passage: Note from Bidisha, class teacher. At lunch, Lakshmi's friend wrinkled her nose while Lakshmi was unpacking her tiffin. Lakshmi shut the box and stopped eating. I sat beside her and asked quietly what was wrong. She said, “She thinks my food smells.” I asked the friend, gently, what the face was about. She said the bin near their bench smelled sour. Lakshmi opened the box again. I suggested to them that when a face worries you, you can ask, “Was that about my food?” They tried the sentence together.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi do after her friend wrinkled her nose?
qa.a: She shut the box and stopped eating.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi probably feeling when she shut her tiffin, and what else could the friend's face have meant?
qa.a: Probably hurt and self-conscious, thinking her food was being rejected. The friend's face was actually about the sour smell from the bin.

qa.q: What small step did Bidisha suggest for next time?
qa.a: That when a face worries them, they ask something like “Was that about my food?” instead of assuming, and she had them practise it together.

qa.q: How might the friend have felt on learning Lakshmi had been hurt?
qa.a: Probably surprised and sorry, since she did not mean anything by it. She joined in practising the question, which suggests she wanted to make it right.

grounding: A child feels hurt by a wrinkled nose at her lunch; asking kindly avoids assuming rejection.

passage: Thursday. Sharmila's diary. At lunch I opened my tiffin, Ma's fish curry and rice, and Sarika wrinkled her nose. Right away my face went hot. Last year a girl called my lunch smelly, and I ate in the corridor for a week. I nearly closed the lid. But Sarika wasn't even looking at my box. I asked, trying to sound normal, “Is it my fish?” She said, “What? No! Someone's thrown a banana peel in the bin behind you. It stinks.” Then she asked if she could try a bite of the fish. She liked it! Tomorrow I'm bringing extra.

qa.q: What was in Sharmila's tiffin?
qa.a: Sharmila's tiffin had Ma's fish curry and rice.

qa.q: Why did Sharmila's face go hot when Sarika wrinkled her nose?
qa.a: Sharmila felt hurt and embarrassed, remembering being teased about lunch last year and fearing it was happening again.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking kindly, “Is it my fish?”, worked because it showed the smell came from the bin, not the lunch, and led to sharing 😊

qa.q: What did the wrinkled nose really mean for Sarika?
qa.a: Sarika was reacting to the stinking banana peel in the bin, and she was happy to try the fish.

grounding: Shows a child reading a friend's wrinkled nose as dislike of their lunch, and asking kindly to find another cause.

passage: Under the neem tree at the village school, Zeenat unwrapped her roti and her Nani's garlic pickle and held some out to Deepak. His nose wrinkled up, lips pulled back. Zeenat's hand stopped in the air. Her Nani had made it specially, and Zeenat had carried it all the way from the fields. She almost put it away without a word. Instead she asked, “You don't like garlic?” Deepak coughed. “I love garlic. It's the smoke. They're burning stubble past the canal, can't you smell it?” Zeenat sniffed. The air was sharp and grey. Deepak took the pickle, and his nose wrinkled again, at the smoke.

qa.q: Where were they burning stubble?
qa.a: They were burning stubble past the canal.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when her hand stopped in the air?
qa.a: Zeenat felt hurt and let down, thinking Deepak disliked the pickle her Nani had made specially.

qa.q: How did Zeenat avoid assuming rejection?
qa.a: She asked a simple question instead of silently putting the pickle away, which showed the smoke caused the wrinkled nose.

qa.q: What was the lunch break like for Deepak?
qa.a: Deepak was bothered by the sharp stubble smoke and coughing, and had no idea his face looked like dislike of the pickle.

grounding: Shows a child reading a friend's wrinkled nose as rejection of their food, and asking kindly to find the real cause.

passage: In Hiroshi's second week at the school in Nairobi, he unwrapped his onigiri at the lunch table. Wanjiru, beside him, wrinkled her nose and turned her face away. Hiroshi's shoulders came up. At his old school, a boy had pinched his nose at this same seaweed. He started folding the wrapper back over. Then he stopped and asked, very quietly, “Does it smell bad to you?” Wanjiru looked surprised. “Your rice? No! The wall behind us was painted this morning. My head is spinning from it.” She pointed at the shiny wall and the sign. They moved to the window table, and she asked what was inside.

qa.q: When had the wall behind them been painted?
qa.a: The wall behind them was painted that morning.

qa.q: Why did Hiroshi's shoulders come up?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and wary, remembering a boy pinching his nose at the same seaweed at his old school.

qa.q: What went right when Hiroshi asked quietly?
qa.a: Asking brought out the real cause, the fresh paint, and turned a hurtful moment into a shared move and a new friendship.

qa.q: How might Wanjiru feel knowing her face made Hiroshi start to fold his lunch away?
qa.a: Wanjiru would probably feel sorry and glad he asked, since she meant nothing against his food.

grounding: Shows a child reading a classmate's wrinkled nose as dislike of their lunch, and asking kindly to avoid assuming rejection.

passage:
Lunch bell. Parul opened her steel tiffin: Amma's fish curry and rice, still warm. Beside her, Wasim wrinkled his nose and leaned away.

Parul's stomach dropped. She snapped the lid shut. Last year a girl had called her lunch "stinky", and the whole table had laughed. She sat with her hands in her lap for a long minute. Then she made herself ask, "Is it my food?"

Wasim looked confused. "Your food? No! Somebody left their football socks on the window ledge behind us. Can't you smell that?"

Parul sniffed. He was right. She opened the lid again, and Wasim asked if he could try a bite.

qa.q: What was in Parul's tiffin?
qa.a: Amma's fish curry and rice, still warm.

qa.q: Why did Parul snap the lid shut?
qa.a: She felt hurt and embarrassed, fearing Wasim was rejecting her food, because last year a girl had called her lunch "stinky" and everyone laughed.

qa.q: Which choice helped Parul avoid a wrong conclusion?
qa.a: She asked kindly, "Is it my food?", instead of assuming rejection, and found out it was the football socks.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel on learning Parul thought he disliked her lunch?
qa.a: He looks confused and probably a bit sorry, since he was only reacting to the socks; asking for a bite shows he wants her to feel okay.

grounding: It shows a child reading a friend's wrinkled nose as dislike of her lunch and asking kindly instead of assuming rejection.
